content: Intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) is a significant complication associated with premature birth, and post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus (PHH) remains a condition without a satisfactory treatment option. Acetazolamide and furosemide, two diuretic medications that reduce cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) production, have been proposed as non-invasive treatments to manage hydrocephalus and potentially reduce the need for ventriculo-peritoneal (V-P) shunting. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of acetazolamide and furosemide on the dependency for V-P shunting and other complications in infants who develop post-hemorrhagic ventricular dilatation (PHVD). To achieve this, a systematic search of electronic databases, including MEDLINE (from 1966), EMBASE (from 1974), and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), was conducted. PubMed was searched on April 18, 2007, and Issue 2, 2007, of The Cochrane Library was also reviewed. The inclusion criteria for the analysis were randomized or quasi-randomized trials comparing acetazolamide and/or furosemide with standard therapy in infants diagnosed with IVH or PHVD. Data extraction was performed independently by the authors, and the analysis followed the standard methods of the Cochrane Collaboration, utilizing relative risk (RR), risk difference (RD), a fixed-effect model, and sensitivity analyses where applicable. Two trials met the eligibility criteria. One trial included 16 infants, while the other involved 177 infants. Neither study demonstrated a reduction in the risk of requiring a V-P shunt or the combined outcome of V-P shunt placement or death with the use of acetazolamide and furosemide therapy. The larger trial revealed a borderline increase in the risk of motor impairment at one year of age among infants treated with these diuretics (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.02–1.58; RD 0.16, 95% CI 0.02–0.31). However, the treatment did not significantly alter the risk of the combined outcome of developmental delay, disability, or motor impairment among survivors, nor did it affect the combined outcome of death, developmental delay, disability, or impairment at one year. The larger trial also demonstrated that diuretic therapy significantly increased the risk of nephrocalcinosis (RR 5.31, 95% CI 1.90–14.84; RD 0.19, 95% CI 0.09–0.29). This finding was confirmed through meta-analysis. In conclusion, the use of acetazolamide and furosemide for the treatment of post-hemorrhagic ventricular dilatation is neither effective nor safe. These medications cannot be recommended as a therapeutic option for managing post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus.
